prior_work.title: Learning Transferable Visual Models From Natural Language Supervision
prior_work.abstract: State-of-the-art computer vision systems are trained to predict a fixed set of predetermined object categories. This restricted form of supervision limits their generality and usability since additional labeled data is needed to specify any other visual concept. Learning directly from raw text about images is a promising alternative which leverages a much broader source of supervision. We demonstrate that the simple pre-training task of predicting which caption goes with which image is an efficient and scalable way to learn SOTA image representations from scratch on a dataset of 400 million (image, text) pairs collected from the internet. After pre-training, natural language is used to reference learned visual concepts (or describe new ones) enabling zero-shot transfer of the model to downstream tasks. We study the performance of this approach by benchmarking on over 30 different existing computer vision datasets, spanning tasks such as OCR, action recognition in videos, geo-localization, and many types of fine-grained object classification. The model transfers non-trivially to most tasks and is often competitive with a fully supervised baseline without the need for any dataset specific training. For instance, we match the accuracy of the original ResNet-50 on ImageNet zero-shot without needing to use any of the 1.28 million training examples it was trained on. We release our code and pre-trained model weights at https://github.com/OpenAI/CLIP.

prior_work.title: EV-SegNet: Semantic Segmentation for Event-based Cameras
prior_work.abstract: Event cameras, or Dynamic Vision Sensor (DVS), are very promising sensors which have shown several advantages over frame based cameras. However, most recent work on real applications of these cameras is focused on 3D reconstruction and 6-DOF camera tracking. Deep learning based approaches, which are leading the state-of-the-art in visual recognition tasks, could potentially take advantage of the benefits of DVS, but some adaptations are needed still needed in order to effectively work on these cameras. This work introduces a first baseline for semantic segmentation with this kind of data. We build a semantic segmentation CNN based on state-of-the-art techniques which takes event information as the only input. Besides, we propose a novel representation for DVS data that outperforms previously used event representations for related tasks. Since there is no existing labeled dataset for this task, we propose how to automatically generate approximated semantic segmentation labels for some sequences of the DDD17 dataset, which we publish together with the model, and demonstrate they are valid to train a model for DVS data only. We compare our results on semantic segmentation from DVS data with results using corresponding grayscale images, demonstrating how they are complementary and worth combining.

prior_work.title: Event-based Vision: A Survey
prior_work.abstract: Event cameras are bio-inspired sensors that differ from conventional frame cameras: Instead of capturing images at a fixed rate, they asynchronously measure per-pixel brightness changes, and output a stream of events that encode the time, location and sign of the brightness changes. Event cameras offer attractive properties compared to traditional cameras: high temporal resolution (in the order of microseconds), very high dynamic range (140 dB vs. 60 dB), low power consumption, and high pixel bandwidth (on the order of kHz) resulting in reduced motion blur. Hence, event cameras have a large potential for robotics and computer vision in challenging scenarios for traditional cameras, such as low-latency, high speed, and high dynamic range. However, novel methods are required to process the unconventional output of these sensors in order to unlock their potential. This paper provides a comprehensive overview of the emerging field of event-based vision, with a focus on the applications and the algorithms developed to unlock the outstanding properties of event cameras. We present event cameras from their working principle, the actual sensors that are available and the tasks that they have been used for, from low-level vision (feature detection and tracking, optic flow, etc.) to high-level vision (reconstruction, segmentation, recognition). We also discuss the techniques developed to process events, including learning-based techniques, as well as specialized processors for these novel sensors, such as spiking neural networks. Additionally, we highlight the challenges that remain to be tackled and the opportunities that lie ahead in the search for a more efficient, bio-inspired way for machines to perceive and interact with the world.

prior_work.title: ESS: Learning Event-based Semantic Segmentation from Still Images
prior_work.abstract: Retrieving accurate semantic information in challenging high dynamic range (HDR) and high-speed conditions remains an open challenge for image-based algorithms due to severe image degradations. Event cameras promise to address these challenges since they feature a much higher dynamic range and are resilient to motion blur. Nonetheless, semantic segmentation with event cameras is still in its infancy which is chiefly due to the lack of high-quality, labeled datasets. In this work, we introduce ESS (Event-based Semantic Segmentation), which tackles this problem by directly transferring the semantic segmentation task from existing labeled image datasets to unlabeled events via unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA). Compared to existing UDA methods, our approach aligns recurrent, motion-invariant event embeddings with image embeddings. For this reason, our method neither requires video data nor per-pixel alignment between images and events and, crucially, does not need to hallucinate motion from still images. Additionally, we introduce DSEC-Semantic, the first large-scale event-based dataset with fine-grained labels. We show that using image labels alone, ESS outperforms existing UDA approaches, and when combined with event labels, it even outperforms state-of-the-art supervised approaches on both DDD17 and DSEC-Semantic. Finally, ESS is general-purpose, which unlocks the vast amount of existing labeled image datasets and paves the way for new and exciting research directions in new fields previously inaccessible for event cameras.

Sb1b857b990c6.title: Text organization via projection from researcher‐space onto text‐space
attribution_passages: Purpose The purpose of this paper is to propose a new approach for organizing texts for researchers based on projection from researcher space (consisting of reasoning ability and research ability) onto text space (consisting of text features). Design/methodology/approach The projection from researcher space onto text space is performed on the grounds of the differences between the sets of essential text features which are consistent, respectively, for the reasoning ability (as researcher's existing ability) and the research ability (as researcher's desired ability) using the concept of a dependency graph. Findings Through the projection from researcher space onto text space, one can expect to find an effective text which can help a person with certain reasoning ability acquire a certain research ability in the related domain. Research limitations/implications Acquisition of reasoning ability (ies) may call for a comprehensive questionnaire or test protocol whose validation by the expert may not necessarily be convenient. Appropriate questionnaires/test protocols, as well as knowledge‐based models for the text features at different layers (to assure derivation of more reliable features), is suggested as future work. Practical implications A salient benefit of the proposed approach is its flexibility in responding to a wide range of users with different models. It thus can be used as an efficient tool for online e‐learning and e‐research purposes in cyber‐learning environment. Originality/value The originality of the paper mostly lies in the concept of projection from researcher space onto text space as an approach for provision of appropriate text features; and the application of dependency graph as a potential means for identifying those text features whose prerequisites exist in the research abilities of the researcher.

Despite CLIP being the foundation model in numerous vision-language applications, the CLIP suffers from a severe text spotting bias. Such bias causes CLIP models to `Parrot' the visual text embedded within images while disregarding the authentic visual semantics. We uncover that in the most popular image-text dataset LAION-2B, the captions also densely parrot (spell) the text embedded in images. Our analysis shows that around 50% of images are embedded with visual text content, and around 30% of captions words are in these embedded visual content. Based on such observation, we thoroughly inspect the different released versions of CLIP models and verify that the visual text is the dominant factor in measuring the LAION-style image-text similarity for these models. To examine whether these parrot captions shape the text spotting bias, we train a series of CLIP models with LAION subsets curated by different parrot-caption-oriented criteria. We show that training with parrot captions easily shapes such bias but harms the expected visual-language representation learning in CLIP models. This suggests that it is urgent to revisit either the design of CLIP-like models or the existing image-text dataset curation pipeline built on CLIP score filtering.

We uncover that in the most popular image-text dataset LAION-2B, the captions also densely parrot (spell) the text embedded in images. Our analysis shows that around 50% of images are embedded with visual text content, and around 30% of captions words are in these embedded visual content. Based on such observation, we thoroughly inspect the different released versions of CLIP models and verify that the visual text is the dominant factor in measuring the LAION-style image-text similarity for these models. To examine whether these parrot captions shape the text spotting bias, we train a series of CLIP models with LAION subsets curated by different parrot-caption-oriented criteria. We show that training with parrot captions easily shapes such bias but harms the expected visual-language representation learning in CLIP models. This suggests that it is urgent to revisit either the design of CLIP-like models or the existing image-text dataset curation pipeline built on CLIP score filtering.

S9094d17f9fab.title: Learning Transferable Visual Models From Natural Language Supervision
S9094d17f9fab.fulltext_snippet: State-of-the-art computer vision systems are trained to predict a fixed set of predetermined object categories. This restricted form of supervision limits their generality and usability since additional labeled data is needed to specify any other visual concept. Learning directly from raw text about images is a promising alternative which leverages a much broader source of supervision. We demonstrate that the simple pre-training task of predicting which caption goes with which image is an efficient and scalable way to learn SOTA image representations from scratch on a dataset of 400 million (image, text) pairs collected from the internet. After pre-training, natural language is used to reference learned visual concepts (or describe new ones) enabling zero-shot transfer of the model to downstream tasks. We study the performance of this approach by benchmarking on over 30 different existing computer vision datasets, spanning tasks such as OCR, action recognition in videos, geo-localization, and many types of fine-grained object classification. The model transfers non-trivially to most tasks and is often competitive with a fully supervised baseline without the need for any dataset specific training. For instance, we match the accuracy of the original ResNet-50 on ImageNet zero-shot without needing to use any of the 1.28 million training examples it was trained on. We release our code and pre-trained model weights at https://github.com/OpenAI/CLIP.

S5a87786ac17e.title: EV-SegNet: Semantic Segmentation for Event-based Cameras
S5a87786ac17e.fulltext_snippet: Event cameras, or Dynamic Vision Sensor (DVS), are very promising sensors which have shown several advantages over frame based cameras. However, most recent work on real applications of these cameras is focused on 3D reconstruction and 6-DOF camera tracking. Deep learning based approaches, which are leading the state-of-the-art in visual recognition tasks, could potentially take advantage of the benefits of DVS, but some adaptations are needed still needed in order to effectively work on these cameras. This work introduces a first baseline for semantic segmentation with this kind of data. We build a semantic segmentation CNN based on state-of-the-art techniques which takes event information as the only input. Besides, we propose a novel representation for DVS data that outperforms previously used event representations for related tasks. Since there is no existing labeled dataset for this task, we propose how to automatically generate approximated semantic segmentation labels for some sequences of the DDD17 dataset, which we publish together with the model, and demonstrate they are valid to train a model for DVS data only. We compare our results on semantic segmentation from DVS data with results using corresponding grayscale images, demonstrating how they are complementary and worth combining.

S2adbd5efdf2b.title: Event-based Vision: A Survey
S2adbd5efdf2b.fulltext_snippet: Event cameras are bio-inspired sensors that differ from conventional frame cameras: Instead of capturing images at a fixed rate, they asynchronously measure per-pixel brightness changes, and output a stream of events that encode the time, location and sign of the brightness changes. Event cameras offer attractive properties compared to traditional cameras: high temporal resolution (in the order of microseconds), very high dynamic range (140 dB vs. 60 dB), low power consumption, and high pixel bandwidth (on the order of kHz) resulting in reduced motion blur. Hence, event cameras have a large potential for robotics and computer vision in challenging scenarios for traditional cameras, such as low-latency, high speed, and high dynamic range. However, novel methods are required to process the unconventional output of these sensors in order to unlock their potential. This paper provides a comprehensive overview of the emerging field of event-based vision, with a focus on the applications and the algorithms developed to unlock the outstanding properties of event cameras. We present event cameras from their working principle, the actual sensors that are available and the tasks that they have been used for, from low-level vision (feature detection and tracking, optic flow, etc.) to high-level vision (reconstruction, segmentation, recognition). We also discuss the techniques developed to process events, including learning-based techniques, as well as specialized processors for these novel sensors, such as spiking neural networks. Additionally, we highlight the challenges that remain to be tackled and the opportunities that lie ahead in the search for a more efficient, bio-inspired way for machines to perceive and interact with the world.

Sda758f8b2f8d.title: ESS: Learning Event-based Semantic Segmentation from Still Images
Sda758f8b2f8d.fulltext_snippet: Retrieving accurate semantic information in challenging high dynamic range (HDR) and high-speed conditions remains an open challenge for image-based algorithms due to severe image degradations. Event cameras promise to address these challenges since they feature a much higher dynamic range and are resilient to motion blur. Nonetheless, semantic segmentation with event cameras is still in its infancy which is chiefly due to the lack of high-quality, labeled datasets. In this work, we introduce ESS (Event-based Semantic Segmentation), which tackles this problem by directly transferring the semantic segmentation task from existing labeled image datasets to unlabeled events via unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA). Compared to existing UDA methods, our approach aligns recurrent, motion-invariant event embeddings with image embeddings. For this reason, our method neither requires video data nor per-pixel alignment between images and events and, crucially, does not need to hallucinate motion from still images. Additionally, we introduce DSEC-Semantic, the first large-scale event-based dataset with fine-grained labels. We show that using image labels alone, ESS outperforms existing UDA approaches, and when combined with event labels, it even outperforms state-of-the-art supervised approaches on both DDD17 and DSEC-Semantic. Finally, ESS is general-purpose, which unlocks the vast amount of existing labeled image datasets and paves the way for new and exciting research directions in new fields previously inaccessible for event cameras.

Sb1b857b990c6.title: Text organization via projection from researcher‐space onto text‐space
Sb1b857b990c6.fulltext_snippet: Purpose The purpose of this paper is to propose a new approach for organizing texts for researchers based on projection from researcher space (consisting of reasoning ability and research ability) onto text space (consisting of text features). Design/methodology/approach The projection from researcher space onto text space is performed on the grounds of the differences between the sets of essential text features which are consistent, respectively, for the reasoning ability (as researcher's existing ability) and the research ability (as researcher's desired ability) using the concept of a dependency graph. Findings Through the projection from researcher space onto text space, one can expect to find an effective text which can help a person with certain reasoning ability acquire a certain research ability in the related domain. Research limitations/implications Acquisition of reasoning ability (ies) may call for a comprehensive questionnaire or test protocol whose validation by the expert may not necessarily be convenient. Appropriate questionnaires/test protocols, as well as knowledge‐based models for the text features at different layers (to assure derivation of more reliable features), is suggested as future work. Practical implications A salient benefit of the proposed approach is its flexibility in responding to a wide range of users with different models. It thus can be used as an efficient tool for online e‐learning and e‐research purposes in cyber‐learning environment. Originality/value The originality of the paper mostly lies in the concept of projection from researcher space onto text space as an approach for provision of appropriate text features; and the application of dependency graph as a potential means for identifying those text features whose prerequisites exist in the research abilities of the researcher.

S2f6155d57d13.title: CLIP-based Cycle Alignment Hashing for unsupervised vision-text retrieval
S2f6155d57d13.fulltext_snippet: Abstract Thanks to the short storage cost and fast retrieval efficiency of hashing methods, deep hashing models are now widely used in cross-modal retrieval. However, the images are often accompanied by correspondingtextual descriptions rather than labels about the vision. So unsupervised cross-modal hash retrieval has received continued widespreadattention. In this paper, we propose CLIP-based Cycle AlignmentHashing for unsupervised vision-text retrieval (CCAH), which aimsto exploit the semantic link between the original features of modalities and the reconstructed features. Firstly we design a modal cyclicinteraction method that aligns semantically within a modality, whereone modal feature reconstructs another modal feature, thus taking full account of the semantic similarity between intra-modal andinter-modal relationships. Secondly, introducing GAT into cross-modalretrieval tasks. Consider the influence of text neighbour nodes and addattention mechanisms to capture the global features of text modalities.Thirdly, Fine-grained extraction of image features using the CLIP visual coder. Finally, hash encoding is learning through hash functions.The experiments demonstrate on three widely used datasets that ourproposed CCAH achieves satisfactory results in total retrieval accuracy.

Sdfb8770a5f00.title: CCAH: a CLIP-based Cycle Alignment Hashing method for unsupervised vision-text retrieval
Sdfb8770a5f00.fulltext_snippet: Abstract Due to the advantages of low storage cost and fast retrieval efficiency, deep hashing methods are widely used in cross-modal retrieval. Images are usually accompanied by corresponding text descriptions rather than labels. Therefore, unsupervised methods have been widely concerned. However, due to the modal divide and semantic differences, existing unsupervised methods cannot adequately bridge the modal differences, leading to suboptimal retrieval results. In this paper, we propose CLIPbased Cycle Alignment Hashing for unsupervised vision-text retrieval (CCAH), which aims to exploit the semantic link between the original features of modalities and the reconstructed features. Firstly we design a modal cyclic interaction method that aligns semantically within intramodality, where one modal feature reconstructs another modal feature, thus taking full account of the semantic similarity between intra-modal and inter-modal relationships. Secondly, introducing GAT into crossmodal retrieval tasks. Consider the influence of text neighbour nodes and add attention mechanisms to capture the global features of text modalities. Thirdly, Fine-grained extraction of image features using the CLIP visual coder. Finally, hash encoding is learning through hash functions. The experiments demonstrate on three widely used datasets that our proposed CCAH achieves satisfactory results in total retrieval accuracy. Our code can be found at :https://github.com/CQYIO/CCAH.git.

draft.title: Open-Vocabulary Event-Based Semantic Segmentation via CLIP-Aligned Event Adapters
draft.literature_gap: Event-based semantic segmentation methods such as EV-SegNet and ESS are closed-vocabulary: they require labeled event datasets for every target class and cannot recognize unseen categories. CLIP provides open-vocabulary visual recognition through natural-language prompts, but it operates on frame-based RGB images and has no mechanism for asynchronous event streams. The missing capability is a method that aligns event-derived dense features to a vision-language embedding space so that event segmentation can generalize to novel classes specified only by text, without collecting new event labels for those classes.
draft.hypothesis: A lightweight event encoder trained with a projection into CLIP's text-embedding space on a small set of seen classes can produce dense event features that classify unseen classes via cosine similarity to their CLIP text embeddings, achieving above-chance zero-shot mIoU on held-out event-segmentation classes.
draft.method: Use event voxel-grid representations from public event datasets (DSEC-Semantic and DDD17 with approximate labels). Train a small event encoder (e.g., ResNet-18-style CNN or tiny ViT) plus a linear/MLP projection to CLIP embedding dimension. For seen classes, compute pixel-wise logits as cosine similarity between projected event features and CLIP text embeddings of class-name prompts, and train with cross-entropy on event semantic labels. Optionally add a contrastive alignment loss to CLIP image embeddings on sequences with paired RGB frames. At inference for open-vocabulary evaluation, replace seen-class text embeddings with embeddings of unseen class names and perform dense nearest-text classification. No labels for unseen classes are used.
draft.minimal_test: Split the public DSEC-Semantic classes into a seen set and a disjoint unseen set (e.g., 8 seen classes, 3 unseen classes; exact split fixed before training). Train the event adapter only on seen-class event labels. Evaluate zero-shot mIoU on the unseen classes using only CLIP text embeddings. Compare against (i) a no-adapter baseline that applies CLIP text embeddings directly to raw event-voxel features, and (ii) chance-level per-pixel assignment among unseen classes. Also report seen-class mIoU to check for catastrophic forgetting.
draft.decisive_metric: Zero-shot mIoU on the held-out unseen classes. Success is declared if the adapter beats the no-adapter baseline by at least 5 mIoU points and exceeds chance by at least 5 points, while retaining at least 80% of the closed-vocabulary seen-class mIoU.
draft.supporting_result: The CLIP-aligned event adapter achieves >15% zero-shot mIoU on unseen DSEC-Semantic classes, improves over the no-adapter event-CLIP baseline by >5 mIoU points, and retains >80% of seen-class closed-vocabulary mIoU.
draft.falsifying_result: Zero-shot unseen-class mIoU is at or below chance, fails to improve over the no-adapter event-CLIP baseline by at least 2 mIoU points, or seen-class mIoU collapses below 50% of the closed-vocabulary baseline.
draft.limitations: DSEC-Semantic has a limited number of classes and may not represent truly broad open-vocabulary conditions. DDD17 labels are approximate, introducing label noise. The adapter is trained on event data only and may inherit CLIP's text-prompt sensitivity and biases. The evaluation uses a fixed seen/unseen split, so results may vary across splits. No new event data or human labels will be collected.
draft.resource_plan: Use only public datasets (DSEC-Semantic, DDD17) and public pretrained CLIP ViT-B/32 weights. Train on a single 24–48 GB GPU for 3–5 days, with total compute under 500 GPU-hours. No annotation budget is required. Code and evaluation scripts will be released; the minimal test uses one fixed class split and three random seeds.

draft.title: EventCLIP-Seg: Aligning Simulated Motion with Frozen CLIP for Open-Vocabulary Event Segmentation
draft.hypothesis: Event streams contain sufficient shape and motion cues for open-vocabulary segmentation if a lightweight event encoder is patch-aligned to CLIP's frozen visual embedding space using physically simulated events and unlabeled real event-RGB pairs. Directly converting events to event frames and applying CLIP fails mainly because of patch-level modality misalignment, not because event data lack semantic information.
draft.related_work: CLIP [S9094d17f9fab] provides strong open-vocabulary image recognition but assumes RGB appearance. Existing event segmentation methods such as EV-SegNet [S5a87786ac17e] and ESS [Sda758f8b2f8d] are closed-set and require dense semantic labels or image-to-event distillation. EventCLIP-style work adapts CLIP to event recognition, but only at the global clip/video level, not for dense spatial segmentation. Recent open-vocabulary RGB methods such as SegCLIP aggregate ViT patches with learnable centers and superpixel losses, while modality-adaptation methods such as MADM use text-to-image diffusion and pseudo-labels to transfer image segmentation to event data; both remain RGB-centric or closed-set. Our proposal differs by learning dense patch-level event-to-CLIP alignment without any semantic labels on events, using simulated motion and unlabeled real event-RGB pairs, then performing zero-shot region-level text matching. It is not a trivial extension of EventCLIP because it targets dense spatial correspondence, event sparsity, and open-vocabulary region segmentation rather than global event classification.
draft.approach: Event cameras offer high dynamic range and microsecond temporal resolution, but event-based semantic segmentation remains closed-set and label-hungry. We introduce EventCLIP-Seg, a label-free framework for open-vocabulary event segmentation. EventCLIP-Seg trains a lightweight event adapter that maps event voxel grids into the frozen CLIP visual patch-embedding space. Supervision comes from physically simulated events generated from images or videos with known camera motion, as well as from unlabeled real event-RGB pairs: corresponding event and RGB patches are aligned contrastively, while CLIP text embeddings provide class semantics only at inference time. To handle event sparsity and noisy boundaries, we aggregate patch-text similarities over class-agnostic superpixels computed from event density and time-surface representations, and we use motion-aware prompt ensembles. At test time, arbitrary text prompts can be matched to event regions, enabling zero-shot segmentation of unseen classes. We build an open-vocabulary benchmark on public event datasets such as DSEC-Semantic and Event-Cityscapes with base/novel class splits. Our central hypothesis is that patch-level cross-modal alignment, rather than pixel-level event-to-RGB reconstruction, is sufficient to bridge events and language. Experiments will compare against event-frame CLIP, global EventCLIP, supervised ESS, and RGB open-vocabulary segmentation baselines, with ablations on simulation, prompt design, temporal aggregation, and superpixel refinement.
draft.validation[1]: Benchmark construction: use DSEC-Semantic real events and Event-Cityscapes simulated events generated from Cityscapes with public labels. Define base/novel class splits (e.g., 10 base and 10 novel classes) with sequence-level train/test separation. Evaluate zero-shot segmentation on novel classes and optional few-shot adaptation on base classes. Metrics: mIoU on seen and unseen classes, harmonic mean, pixel accuracy, and per-class IoU.
draft.validation[2]: Adapter training without semantic labels: convert event streams to 5-bin voxel grids with polarity channels; use a small event encoder (ViT-S or ConvNeXt-T) and a linear/MLP projection to CLIP's patch-embedding dimension. Generate simulated events from COCO/ImageNet frames or short videos using v2e/ESIM with random affine camera motion. Also use unlabeled real event-RGB pairs from DSEC training sequences. Train only the adapter with patch-wise and global contrastive losses against frozen CLIP visual embeddings; no event semantic labels are used.
draft.validation[3]: Open-vocabulary inference: compute patch-level similarity between adapted event features and CLIP text embeddings using prompt ensembles such as 'an event camera recording of a {class}', 'motion boundaries of a {class}', and 'edges of a {class}'. Aggregate patch scores over class-agnostic superpixels obtained by SLIC on event-density and time-surface images. Add optional test-time calibration using a background prior and entropy-based confidence.
draft.validation[4]: Baselines: compare with (a) direct event-frame CLIP/CLIPSeg/OVSeg, (b) EventCLIP global recognition followed by sliding-window dense prediction, (c) supervised ESS trained on base classes, (d) event-to-image translation followed by RGB open-vocabulary segmentation, and (e) an oracle supervised event segmentation model.
draft.validation[5]: Ablations and robustness: test synthetic-only vs real-only vs combined alignment; patch-level vs global-only contrastive alignment; different event representations (voxel grid, time surface, polarity-separated frames); temporal bin counts; prompt template choices; superpixel aggregation vs dense patch upsampling; and simulation realism. Evaluate under low-light/HDR conditions, high-speed motion, and cross-dataset transfer DSEC to Event-Cityscapes. Analyze failure cases involving static objects, very sparse events, small objects, and classes distinguished mainly by color/texture rather than shape or motion.
draft.validation[6]: Efficiency study: report adapter training cost, inference latency, and memory. The method freezes CLIP and trains only a small adapter, making it feasible for an academic lab using public datasets and a single or few GPUs.
draft.limitations[1]: Simulation-to-reality gap: synthetic events from v2e/ESIM may not perfectly match real sensor noise, refractory periods, and threshold variations, causing negative transfer.
draft.limitations[2]: Event sparsity: static or slowly moving objects produce few events, making dense semantic inference fundamentally ambiguous and limiting CLIP-like appearance cues.
draft.limitations[3]: CLIP patch features are coarse and RGB-biased; patch-level alignment may not provide sufficiently sharp boundaries, and superpixel aggregation may propagate errors.
draft.limitations[4]: Prompt sensitivity: open-vocabulary performance depends heavily on class-name choice and prompt templates, and event-specific prompts may introduce unintended biases.
draft.limitations[5]: Real event-RGB pairs require calibration and temporal synchronization; imperfect correspondence can add noise to contrastive alignment.
draft.limitations[6]: No standard open-vocabulary event segmentation benchmark exists, so base/novel class splits and evaluation protocols must be carefully justified to avoid cherry-picking.
draft.limitations[7]: The adapter may overfit to training sequences or camera biases, reducing cross-dataset generalization.
draft.limitations[8]: Classes discriminated mainly by color or fine texture may remain difficult because event streams encode brightness changes rather than absolute appearance.

draft.claims[1].text: Supplied CLIP evidence states that, given a batch of N image-text pairs, CLIP is trained to predict which of the N×N possible pairings actually occurred; this supports a contrastive alignment premise only under those stated conditions.
draft.claims[2].text: Supplied E2VID evidence characterizes E2VID as a zero-shot UDA baseline that cannot be retrained for a specific target domain.
draft.claims[3].text: Supplied parrot-caption evidence reports conditions under which captions contain words concurrent with visual text in images, so maximizing image-text similarity can be satisfied by text spotting rather than visual-language semantic alignment.
draft.claims[4].text: Supplied evidence reports that released CLIP models show strong text-spotting bias on web images, contributing to bias in CLIP-filtering datasets toward visual-text-dominant data.
draft.claims[5].text: Supplied LAION-2B statement reports that over 90% of captions have at least one concurrent word with spotted image text, with at least around 30% word overlap.
draft.claims[6].text: Supplied evidence reports that training on parrot-caption subsets yields text-spotting capacity but degrades zero-shot generalization on image-text downstream tasks under the reported setting.
draft.claims[7].text: Supplied DSEC-Semantic UDA evidence reports that omitting an embedding-space consistency loss causes a 5.56% mIoU drop in that reported setting; this supports the consistency-term design premise but is not a result of this Proposal.
draft.claims[8].text: Supplied event-representation evidence reports that encoding event histogram and temporal distribution improved semantic segmentation in its experiments; this Proposal treats that as a labeled design assumption, not as established for the proposed study.
draft.claims[9].text: Supplied E2VID evidence reports that motion-invariant event embeddings retain semantic information for segmentation under labeled-source and unlabeled-event conditions.
draft.claims[10].text: This is a newly specified prospective design and is not a faithful replication of CLIP or E2VID; no experiment, computation, data acquisition, audit result, or numerical outcome is claimed.
draft.gap: Supplied evidence reports that E2VID is a zero-shot UDA baseline that cannot be retrained for a specific target domain, that an embedding-space consistency loss improved event-image alignment in a DSEC-Semantic UDA setting, and that CLIP-style image-text contrastive training can be satisfied by text-spotting and parrot-caption shortcuts under stated conditions. It is not established that event-region embeddings can be aligned to frozen text prototypes for unseen labels, that semantic information survives event-specific shifts, or that any held-out gain is not closed-set fitting. The expected knowledge increment is a pre-registered, matched-control test of those unresolved bridges and a claim-scope rule that separates open-vocabulary transfer from closed-set-like behavior; positive, negative, or uncertain outcomes would each be informative.
draft.idea: Use event-derived spatiotemporal regions, an event-adapted image encoder initialized from still-to-event transfer in an E2VID-style but newly specified variant, and frozen text prototypes for label names aligned by a CLIP-style contrastive objective trained only on seen labels. Add an event-view consistency term across noise, motion, and resolution perturbations. Bound the interpretable claim with a frozen public-resource identity/no-download gate, a pre-registered prototype-shortcut audit, matched closed-set and trivial-prior controls, shuffled-prototype and no-text-alignment controls, co-primary seen-vocabulary and calibration measures, event-shift stress conditions, component-isolation comparisons, and a claim-scope rule. This is a newly specified prospective method, not a faithful replication of CLIP or E2VID.
draft.method[1]: Design definition and scope: this is a prospective, newly specified method, not a faithful replication of CLIP or E2VID. It addresses rq-1 and rq-2, with the primary claim on held-out unseen-vocabulary event segmentation under nominal events; seen-vocabulary mIoU and calibration are co-primary controls. No experiment or computation is executed in this artifact, and no numerical result is claimed.
draft.method[2]: Frozen resource-identity block and no-download gate: before any download, installation, pretraining, prompt tuning, or modeling, record a resource-identity block containing the exact public dataset release/tag, license, checksum, frozen split-file SHA-256, event preprocessing version, image-encoder version and checksum, text-encoder and tokenizer version and checksum, and prompt-ensemble version. Candidate data must match the supplied DSEC-Semantic UDA condition: public event-camera semantic segmentation data with labeled source images and unlabeled target event streams. The exact public release/tag, license, and checksum are not supplied in this packet, are not asserted as verified, and are required evidence and a Preparation gate.
draft.method[3]: Pre-registered public fallback rule: if no exact public DSEC-Semantic release/tag can be verified from public documentation, select a fallback before download by a deterministic rule. The fallback must be public, have pixel-level semantic annotations and canonical label names, provide labeled source images and unlabeled target event streams in a UDA-compatible structure, have a public release tag, checksum, and a license permitting the planned research use, and support the same event-camera semantic-label structure. Among candidates satisfying these criteria, sort by SHA-256 of 'canonical dataset name|release tag|license' and choose the smallest hash. Record the exact identity and freeze the split-file SHA-256 before any download or modeling. If no candidate satisfies the criteria, stop; do not silently substitute another population.
draft.method[4]: Vocabulary splits: after the resource-identity block is frozen, use the dataset canonical label-name list, lowercase and trim names, and apply only the dataset-provided synonym mapping. Sort canonical names by their SHA-256 hex string; assign names whose first byte is <128 to held-out H and the rest to seen S. If either set has fewer than 5 classes, deterministically move the next hash-ordered name from the larger set to the smaller until both have at least 5. Freeze the split file and its SHA-256 before model selection. Training, model selection, calibration fitting, and prompt tuning may use S only; H labels and target labels are excluded from those steps.
draft.method[5]: Shared event preprocessing: all method and control conditions use one identical event tensor per 50 ms window with channels for positive event count, negative event count, mean timestamp, last timestamp, and log event density. Resample to a fixed sensor grid by nearest-neighbor; apply the same annotation-derived ignore mask and normalization to every condition. Perturbations are applied to raw events before this shared tensorization.
draft.method[6]: Event-region construction: in each window, form regions from connected components of event density above a fixed per-window threshold equal to the 80th percentile of nonzero event-density pixels; merge components within 3 pixels; record bounding box and event statistics. Region proposals are deterministic and shared across method and controls.
draft.method[7]: Frozen text prototypes and shortcut boundary: the event-adapted image encoder is initialized from a public still-image encoder and trained with an E2VID-style event-to-image reconstruction auxiliary as a newly specified transfer variant. Frozen text prototypes come from a public CLIP-style text encoder using the prompt ensemble a photo of a {label} in an event camera scene. Compute prototypes for S and H before training; only S prototypes enter the alignment loss. Supplied CLIP evidence supports image-text contrastive alignment when pairs co-occur; supplied E2VID evidence reports motion-invariant event embeddings that retain semantic information under labeled-source and unlabeled-event conditions. Supplied shortcut evidence shows that co-occurrence-driven contrastive objectives can be satisfied by text-spotting and parrot-caption shortcuts and that training on such data can lose zero-shot generalization. Therefore the premise that frozen text prototypes encode semantics for unseen labels is bounded, not established for event data; the audit and controls below limit the interpretable claim.
draft.method[8]: Pre-registered prototype-shortcut audit, planned and not executed: before any model selection, training, prompt tuning, or evaluation, freeze the H/S split and a deterministic control-string list. For each frozen label name, generate controls by fixed rules: character-scrambled label names with the identical multiset of characters, the strings a photo of printed text saying {label} and a photo of a sign reading {label}, and a length-matched nonsemantic filler string. Use the same public text encoder, tokenizer, and prompt-ensemble normalization for labels and controls. Report prospectively: mean within-H and between-H/S cosine separability; each H label's nearest non-self prototype among H, S, and control-string prototypes; duplicate and near-duplicate counts at cosine >=0.99; lexical-confound diagnostics including Spearman correlation between pairwise prototype cosine and character n-gram Jaccard overlap; and visual-text-confound diagnostics including mean cosine of H prototypes to printed-text and sign controls relative to distinct H-label prototype similarity. Audit pass rule, fixed before computation: no two distinct H label prototypes have cosine >=0.99; no H label's nearest non-self prototype among H, S, and controls is a control string; the prototype-to-character-n-gram-overlap correlation is <=0.5; and the mean H-prototype similarity to printed-text and sign controls is <=0.5 and at least 0.05 lower than the mean cosine among distinct H label prototypes. These thresholds are pre-specified design assumptions, not empirical estimates. The audit is necessary but not sufficient to exclude an image-side visual-text shortcut; the confirmatory controls below remain required.
draft.method[9]: Alignment objective and training: compute cosine similarity between each event-region embedding and frozen text prototypes, then apply symmetric cross-entropy over S prototypes with in-batch negatives in a CLIP-style contrastive objective. Add an event-view consistency term: symmetric cosine distance between region embeddings of clean and perturbed views, weight lambda=0.1. Training uses S labels only. The prototype-shortcut audit is evaluated before training; its recorded pass or fail status is part of the frozen method record.
draft.method[10]: Matched controls and fairness: the primary closed-set control is an event segmenter with the same event tensor, same encoder family and target parameter count within plus or minus 5 percent, same optimizer budget, same seeds, and training on S only. prior_work.title: PyramidKV: Dynamic KV Cache Compression based on Pyramidal Information Funneling
prior_work.abstract: In this study, we investigate whether attention-based information flow inside large language models (LLMs) is aggregated through noticeable patterns for long context processing. Our observations reveal that LLMs aggregate information through Pyramidal Information Funneling where attention is scattering widely in lower layers, progressively consolidating within specific contexts, and ultimately focusing on critical tokens (a.k.a massive activation or attention sink) in higher layers. Motivated by these insights, we developed PyramidKV, a novel and effective KV cache compression method. This approach dynamically adjusts the KV cache size across different layers, allocating more cache in lower layers and less in higher ones, diverging from traditional methods that maintain a uniform KV cache size. Our experimental evaluations, utilizing the LongBench benchmark, show that PyramidKV matches the performance of models with a full KV cache while retaining only 12% of the KV cache, thus significantly reducing memory usage. In scenarios emphasizing memory efficiency, where only 0.7% of the KV cache is maintained, PyramidKV surpasses other KV cache compression techniques, achieving up to a 20.5 absolute accuracy improvement on TREC dataset. In the Needle-in-a-Haystack experiment, PyramidKV outperforms competing methods in maintaining long-context comprehension in LLMs; notably, retaining just 128 KV cache entries enables the LLAMA-3-70B model to achieve 100.0 Acc. performance.

prior_work.title: DynamicKV: Task-Aware Adaptive KV Cache Compression for Long Context LLMs
prior_work.abstract: Efficient KV cache management in LLMs is crucial for long-context tasks like RAG and summarization. Existing KV cache compression methods enforce a fixed pattern, neglecting task-specific characteristics and reducing the retention of essential information. However, we observe distinct activation patterns across layers in various tasks, highlighting the need for adaptive strategies tailored to each task's unique demands. Based on this insight, we propose DynamicKV, a method that dynamically optimizes token retention by adjusting the number of tokens retained at each layer to adapt to the specific task. DynamicKV establishes global and per-layer maximum KV cache budgets, temporarily retaining the maximum budget for the current layer, and periodically updating the KV cache sizes of all preceding layers during inference. Our method retains only 1.7% of the KV cache size while achieving ~85% of the Full KV cache performance on LongBench. Notably, even under extreme compression (0.9%), DynamicKV surpasses state-of-the-art (SOTA) methods by 11% in the Needle-in-a-Haystack test using Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.2. The code will be released.

prior_work.title: VL-Cache: Sparsity and Modality-Aware KV Cache Compression for Vision-Language Model Inference Acceleration
prior_work.abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have demonstrated impressive performance across a versatile set of tasks. A key challenge in accelerating VLMs is storing and accessing the large Key-Value (KV) cache that encodes long visual contexts, such as images or videos. While existing KV cache compression methods are effective for Large Language Models (LLMs), directly migrating them to VLMs yields suboptimal accuracy and speedup. To bridge the gap, we propose VL-Cache, a novel KV cache compression recipe tailored for accelerating VLM inference. In this paper, we first investigate the unique sparsity pattern of VLM attention by distinguishing visual and text tokens in prefill and decoding phases. Based on these observations, we introduce a layer-adaptive sparsity-aware cache budget allocation method that effectively distributes the limited cache budget across different layers, further reducing KV cache size without compromising accuracy. Additionally, we develop a modality-aware token scoring policy to better evaluate the token importance. Empirical results on multiple benchmark datasets demonstrate that retaining only 10% of KV cache achieves accuracy comparable to that with full cache. In a speed benchmark, our method accelerates end-to-end latency of generating 100 tokens by up to 2.33x and speeds up decoding by up to 7.08x, while reducing the memory footprint of KV cache in GPU by 90%.

S05a64f67982b.title: To collapse or not to collapse: Halo evolution with self-interacting dark matter mass segregation
attribution_passages: Surprisingly compact substructures in galaxies and galaxy clusters, but also field halos, have been observed by gravitational lensing. They could be difficult to explain with collisionless dark matter (DM). To explain those objects, recent studies focused on the gravothermal collapse that halos consisting of self-interacting dark matter (SIDM) can undergo. However, simple models of elastic scattering could face problems explaining those compact objects during very later stages of the collapse and the post-collapse phase, where a black hole may have formed from DM. We aim to explain compact halos while avoiding the gravothermal catastrophe to which typical SIDM models are subject. Therefore, we investigate the evolution of a DM halo for an SIDM model consisting of two species with unequal masses, which features only interactions between the different species but not within themselves. Employing $N$-body simulations, we study the effect of unequal-mass SIDM models on the evolution of an isolated DM halo. In particular, the late stages of its evolution with high central densities are simulated. We find that our two-species SIDM models can produce density cores with their size depending on the mass ratio of the two species. Moreover, mass segregation caused by the unequal particle masses leads to a finite final density state or at least a slowly growing density, which depends on the mass ratio and the mass fraction of the two DM species. SIDM models consisting of two DM species can simultaneously explain DM halos with density cores, as well as systems that are denser in their centre than expected from collisionless DM, while avoiding the gravothermal catastrophe. They are a compelling alternative to single-species models, offering a rich phenomenology.

S5ee01c4a726e.title: The Determinants of International Investment and Attention Allocation: Using Internet Search Query Data
attribution_passages: Few studies have successfully examined the empirical impact of limited information processing on real economic variables. The challenge relies, of course, on the difficulty of measuring an economic agent's degree of attention/inattention paid to different types of information. This paper overcomes such challenge exploring a unique dataset containing the "search/click-through" behavior of internet search engine users. We analyzes the effect of attention allocation on international investment decisions by combining U.S. data on portfolio holdings of foreign securities with the attention allocated by 657,426 America Online customers in search queries towards these countries. We find evidence that: (i) agents tend to search more information about countries where they hold more assets, and (ii) agents tend to invest more in countries where they process more information.

attribution_passages: LAVa, however, consistently achieves top performance across both task types and language models.

KV Cache is commonly used to accelerate LLM inference with long contexts, yet its high memory demand drives the need for cache compression. Existing compression methods, however, are largely heuristic and lack dynamic budget allocation. To address this limitation, we introduce a unified framework for cache compression by minimizing information loss in Transformer residual streams. Building on it, we analyze the layer attention output loss and derive a new metric to compare cache entries across heads, enabling layer-wise compression with dynamic head budgets. Additionally, by contrasting cross-layer information, we also achieve dynamic layer budgets. LAVa is the first unified strategy for cache eviction and dynamic budget allocation that, unlike prior methods, does not rely on training or the combination of multiple strategies. Experiments with benchmarks (LongBench, Needle-In-A-Haystack, Ruler, and InfiniteBench) demonstrate its superiority. Moreover, our experiments reveal a new insight: dynamic layer budgets are crucial for generation tasks (e.g., code completion), while dynamic head budgets play a key role in extraction tasks (e.g., extractive QA). As a fully dynamic compression method, LAVa consistently maintains top performance across task types. Our code is available at https://github.com/MGDDestiny/Lava.

S53644328019a.title: PyramidKV: Dynamic KV Cache Compression based on Pyramidal Information Funneling
S53644328019a.fulltext_snippet: In this study, we investigate whether attention-based information flow inside large language models (LLMs) is aggregated through noticeable patterns for long context processing. Our observations reveal that LLMs aggregate information through Pyramidal Information Funneling where attention is scattering widely in lower layers, progressively consolidating within specific contexts, and ultimately focusing on critical tokens (a.k.a massive activation or attention sink) in higher layers. Motivated by these insights, we developed PyramidKV, a novel and effective KV cache compression method. This approach dynamically adjusts the KV cache size across different layers, allocating more cache in lower layers and less in higher ones, diverging from traditional methods that maintain a uniform KV cache size. Our experimental evaluations, utilizing the LongBench benchmark, show that PyramidKV matches the performance of models with a full KV cache while retaining only 12% of the KV cache, thus significantly reducing memory usage. In scenarios emphasizing memory efficiency, where only 0.7% of the KV cache is maintained, PyramidKV surpasses other KV cache compression techniques, achieving up to a 20.5 absolute accuracy improvement on TREC dataset. In the Needle-in-a-Haystack experiment, PyramidKV outperforms competing methods in maintaining long-context comprehension in LLMs; notably, retaining just 128 KV cache entries enables the LLAMA-3-70B model to achieve 100.0 Acc. performance.

Seab945ad8e6d.title: DynamicKV: Task-Aware Adaptive KV Cache Compression for Long Context LLMs
Seab945ad8e6d.fulltext_snippet: Efficient KV cache management in LLMs is crucial for long-context tasks like RAG and summarization. Existing KV cache compression methods enforce a fixed pattern, neglecting task-specific characteristics and reducing the retention of essential information. However, we observe distinct activation patterns across layers in various tasks, highlighting the need for adaptive strategies tailored to each task's unique demands. Based on this insight, we propose DynamicKV, a method that dynamically optimizes token retention by adjusting the number of tokens retained at each layer to adapt to the specific task. DynamicKV establishes global and per-layer maximum KV cache budgets, temporarily retaining the maximum budget for the current layer, and periodically updating the KV cache sizes of all preceding layers during inference. Our method retains only 1.7% of the KV cache size while achieving ~85% of the Full KV cache performance on LongBench. Notably, even under extreme compression (0.9%), DynamicKV surpasses state-of-the-art (SOTA) methods by 11% in the Needle-in-a-Haystack test using Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.2. The code will be released.

Se2fd03004cac.title: VL-Cache: Sparsity and Modality-Aware KV Cache Compression for Vision-Language Model Inference Acceleration
Se2fd03004cac.fulltext_snippet: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have demonstrated impressive performance across a versatile set of tasks. A key challenge in accelerating VLMs is storing and accessing the large Key-Value (KV) cache that encodes long visual contexts, such as images or videos. While existing KV cache compression methods are effective for Large Language Models (LLMs), directly migrating them to VLMs yields suboptimal accuracy and speedup. To bridge the gap, we propose VL-Cache, a novel KV cache compression recipe tailored for accelerating VLM inference. In this paper, we first investigate the unique sparsity pattern of VLM attention by distinguishing visual and text tokens in prefill and decoding phases. Based on these observations, we introduce a layer-adaptive sparsity-aware cache budget allocation method that effectively distributes the limited cache budget across different layers, further reducing KV cache size without compromising accuracy. Additionally, we develop a modality-aware token scoring policy to better evaluate the token importance. Empirical results on multiple benchmark datasets demonstrate that retaining only 10% of KV cache achieves accuracy comparable to that with full cache. In a speed benchmark, our method accelerates end-to-end latency of generating 100 tokens by up to 2.33x and speeds up decoding by up to 7.08x, while reducing the memory footprint of KV cache in GPU by 90%.

S05a64f67982b.title: To collapse or not to collapse: Halo evolution with self-interacting dark matter mass segregation
S05a64f67982b.fulltext_snippet: Surprisingly compact substructures in galaxies and galaxy clusters, but also field halos, have been observed by gravitational lensing. They could be difficult to explain with collisionless dark matter (DM). To explain those objects, recent studies focused on the gravothermal collapse that halos consisting of self-interacting dark matter (SIDM) can undergo. However, simple models of elastic scattering could face problems explaining those compact objects during very later stages of the collapse and the post-collapse phase, where a black hole may have formed from DM. We aim to explain compact halos while avoiding the gravothermal catastrophe to which typical SIDM models are subject. Therefore, we investigate the evolution of a DM halo for an SIDM model consisting of two species with unequal masses, which features only interactions between the different species but not within themselves. Employing $N$-body simulations, we study the effect of unequal-mass SIDM models on the evolution of an isolated DM halo. In particular, the late stages of its evolution with high central densities are simulated. We find that our two-species SIDM models can produce density cores with their size depending on the mass ratio of the two species. Moreover, mass segregation caused by the unequal particle masses leads to a finite final density state or at least a slowly growing density, which depends on the mass ratio and the mass fraction of the two DM species. SIDM models consisting of two DM species can simultaneously explain DM halos with density cores, as well as systems that are denser in their centre than expected from collisionless DM, while avoiding the gravothermal catastrophe. They are a compelling alternative to single-species models, offering a rich phenomenology.

S5ee01c4a726e.title: The Determinants of International Investment and Attention Allocation: Using Internet Search Query Data
S5ee01c4a726e.fulltext_snippet: Few studies have successfully examined the empirical impact of limited information processing on real economic variables. The challenge relies, of course, on the difficulty of measuring an economic agent's degree of attention/inattention paid to different types of information. This paper overcomes such challenge exploring a unique dataset containing the "search/click-through" behavior of internet search engine users. We analyzes the effect of attention allocation on international investment decisions by combining U.S. data on portfolio holdings of foreign securities with the attention allocated by 657,426 America Online customers in search queries towards these countries. We find evidence that: (i) agents tend to search more information about countries where they hold more assets, and (ii) agents tend to invest more in countries where they process more information.

draft.title: Query-Probe Budget Reallocation: Testing Whether Layer-Adaptive KV Cache Compression Survives Multi-Evidence Retrieval
draft.literature_gap: The supplied cache-compression papers establish layer-adaptive and task-adaptive KV budgets: PyramidKV uses pyramidal attention to allocate more cache to lower layers, DynamicKV adjusts per-layer budgets by task, and VL-Cache adds modality-aware allocation for vision-language models. Their evaluations center on LongBench aggregates and Needle-in-a-Haystack, with DynamicKV reporting ~85% of full-cache LongBench performance at 1.7% KV and PyramidKV reporting strong NIAH retention. A visible gap is that none isolates multi-evidence retrieval, where one query requires two or more passages at different context depths, and none tests whether task-level or fixed pyramidal layer budgets remain valid when evidence is split across low-attention layers. Thus it is unknown whether extreme layer-adaptive compression preserves query-specific evidence that is not a single needle and is not well represented by aggregate LongBench scores.
draft.hypothesis: At 1.7% and 0.9% KV budgets, DynamicKV/PyramidKV-style layer-adaptive compression will lose at least 10 absolute exact-match points versus full KV on multi-evidence retrieval examples where two answer-bearing passages are separated by more than half the context. A lightweight query-conditioned prefill attention probe that shifts at most 10% of the total per-layer budget toward layers with high query-to-context attention entropy will recover at least 50% of that lost gap, while a random-probe allocation and a no-query DynamicKV allocation will not.
draft.method: Use the open-weight Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.2 model and public LongBench multi-document QA contexts. Build two evaluation sets: (1) a LongBench multi-document QA subset filtered to examples requiring evidence from at least two passages; (2) a controlled two-needle NIAH set constructed from public LongBench contexts by inserting two answer spans at varied depth pairs (early-late, middle-late, early-middle) with distractor passages between them. No proprietary data or future answer keys are used. Implement three cache policies at fixed global budgets of 1.7% and 0.9%: full KV; DynamicKV as the supplied-paper baseline; PyramidKV as a second supplied-paper baseline; and the proposed Query-Probe Reallocation (QPR). QPR runs a normal prefill, computes per-layer query-to-context attention mass/entropy from a small fixed set of probe heads, and reallocates at most 10% of the total cache budget from low-probe to high-probe layers on top of DynamicKV's task-level budget. Ablations: random probe with the same reallocation magnitude, no-query DynamicKV, and an oracle evidence-position allocation used only as a diagnostic upper bound. All methods use identical prompts and decoding.
draft.minimal_test: Run 300 filtered LongBench multi-document QA examples and 300 controlled two-needle examples with Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.2 under full KV, DynamicKV, PyramidKV, QPR, random-probe QPR, no-query DynamicKV, and oracle allocation at 1.7% and 0.9% budgets. Primary comparison is QPR versus DynamicKV on multi-evidence exact match. Secondary diagnostics are second-needle recall, performance split by whether both evidence spans fall in the bottom attention-mass quartile of layers, and the random-probe ablation. The test is falsifiable because pre-registered thresholds below determine support or failure.
draft.decisive_metric: Primary: multi-evidence exact match at 1.7% KV. Let G = EM(full KV) - EM(DynamicKV) and R = (EM(QPR) - EM(DynamicKV)) / G. Support requires G >= 5 absolute EM points, R >= 0.50, and EM(QPR) - EM(DynamicKV) >= 5 absolute points. Diagnostic: second-needle recall must improve by at least 15 absolute points over DynamicKV, and the random-probe ablation must recover less than half of QPR's gain. At 0.9% KV, the same direction is required but is secondary.
draft.supporting_result: The hypothesis is supported if, at 1.7% KV, DynamicKV loses at least 5 absolute multi-evidence EM points relative to full KV, QPR recovers at least 50% of that gap with at least a 5-point absolute EM gain over DynamicKV, second-needle recall improves by at least 15 points, and the random-probe and no-query ablations fail to match QPR. Supporting evidence would also show errors concentrated in examples where both evidence spans fall in low-attention layers and QPR reduces that failure group.
draft.falsifying_result: The hypothesis is falsified if any of the following occurs at 1.7% KV: full KV and DynamicKV differ by less than 5 absolute multi-evidence EM points, so the multi-evidence failure mode is not material; QPR improves DynamicKV by less than 2 absolute EM points; QPR recovers less than 20% of the full-cache gap; or the random-probe QPR ablation recovers at least 40% of the gap, indicating that query-conditioned probing is not the causal mechanism.

draft.title: The Reuse Tax: Measuring How Much of KV-Cache Compression's Reported Wins Disappear When the Query Is Unknown
draft.hypothesis: Nearly all KV-cache compression methods in this neighborhood (PyramidKV, DynamicKV, LAVa, DefensiveKV, and even PyramidKV's pyramidal-funneling analysis) score and evict cache entries *conditioned on the user's query during prefill*. That is a single-request evaluation protocol. Real retrieval/agentic serving builds one shared-context cache and then answers K diverse queries from it (SCBench, KVLink, APE, MEPIC, CompLLM all show this is the deployment reality). We hypothesize that there exists a large, previously unmeasured **reuse tax**: at matched compression budget, a cache compressed without knowledge of the query retains far less of the accuracy that query-aware compression reports, and the tax grows with query diversity K until the reported Pareto rankings of compression methods reverse under amortized (accuracy per GPU-memory-second over K queries) accounting. A second, cheap diagnostic — the Jaccard overlap of selected KV positions across K queries for the same context — should predict the tax a priori, and a dead-simple query-agnostic baseline (value-activation-norm scoring with a layer budget profile, which also sidesteps the FlashAttention incompatibility that reviewers flagged for attention-score methods like DynamicKV/PyramidKV, and which uses the V-side signal that reviewers flagged as ignored) should shrink it substantially. The test is minimal and falsifiable: if query-aware PyramidKV at 12% budget loses <5% of its own accuracy when the query is hidden at compression time, the hypothesis is dead.
draft.related_work: The supplied neighborhood optimizes compression *given* a query: PyramidKV (pyramidal attention funnels, 12% cache on LongBench), DynamicKV (task-aware per-layer budgets, 1.7% cache, 90/87/78/83% retention across four models), LAVa (layer- and head-dynamic eviction; itself notes layer budgets matter for generation vs head budgets for extraction), DefensiveKV (worst-case-risk aggregation of importance scores against the fragility of the stability assumption), and the 'Preserving Large Activations' paper (value activations matter; reviewers flagged that V-cache variance is unexplained). All are evaluated in LongBench/NIAH/RULER single-request style. Separately, a fast-growing systems cluster assumes query-agnostic, chunk-level, reusable caches: KVLink (precomputed per-document KV + position fixups + trainable link tokens), APE (parallel encoding with shared prefix/temperature/scaling), MEPIC (position-independent block-aligned chunk reuse), CompLLM (segment-wise soft compression explicitly for reusability), EpiCache (episodic query-agnostic eviction for long conversations), and SCBench, which explicitly critiques single-request evaluation and evaluates KV-cache lifecycles with shared contexts. Our proposal is NOT a new compression method and NOT another benchmark: it is a head-to-head *decomposition* of the compression Pareto frontier into (query-aware accuracy) + (reuse tax), at matched budget, plus a predictive diagnostic (cross-query position-overlap) and one deliberately simple query-agnostic baseline. Difference from SCBench: SCBench reports scores of many methods under shared-context modes; it does not isolate the query-aware vs query-agnostic gap at matched budget, does not provide the overlap diagnostic that predicts which methods are reusable, and does not do amortized-over-K accounting. Difference from EpiCache/CompLLM: those are individual systems, not a diagnosis of why the single-request compression literature's numbers fail to transfer. The finding, if true, reframes a whole sub-literature's evaluation and gives practitioners a 5-minute pre-check (overlap) before choosing a compressor for a RAG/agent server.
draft.approach: KV-cache compression papers in this neighborhood report that 1.7%–12% of the cache suffices on LongBench. But they compress *after* seeing the query, while production RAG and agent servers build a shared-context cache *before* any query arrives (KVLink, APE, MEPIC, CompLLM, SCBench all point this out). We propose one minimal falsifiable test: the **reuse tax** — the accuracy a compressor loses when its cache must serve K queries it never saw, relative to its own query-aware accuracy at identical budget. Using one open-weight model (Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, with Qwen2.5-7B as a replication check) and public shared-context multi-query sets built from SCBench/LongBench-v2 plus NIAH, we compress each context once with the query hidden, then answer K∈{1,4,8,16,32} diverse queries, and compare against query-aware compression at matched budget and against the full cache. We additionally compute a zero-cost diagnostic — the Jaccard overlap of selected KV positions across the K queries — and test whether it predicts the tax before any accuracy run. Finally we test a deliberately simple query-agnostic baseline (value-activation-norm scoring with an LAVa/DynamicKV-style layer budget profile, implemented at block granularity so it stays FlashAttention-compatible, addressing reviewer concerns about attention-score methods). Metrics: task accuracy, reuse tax, cross-query overlap, peak KV memory, TTFT, and accuracy per GPU-memory-second amortized over K. Under 8 A100-days, inference-only.
draft.validation: Setup. Open weights only: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (primary) and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct (replication); all inference-only, fp16, A100-80GB, vLLM/SGLang with paged KV plus a PyTorch reference path for exact index bookkeeping. Public data only: SCBench shared-context subsets, LongBench-v2 multi-document/QA subsets, and a synthetic NIAH variant. Build M multi-query bundles: each bundle = one long context (8k–64k tokens) + K=32 human/synthesized queries that are answerable from that context and are deliberately diverse (different answer spans, different evidence sections; verify via gold spans and a diversity check on answer-span location). Total ~300 bundles. (1) MATCHED-BUDGET REUSE TAX (core falsification test). Baselines from supplied papers reimplemented at their reported budgets: PyramidKV (12%), DynamicKV (1.7% and 5%), LAVa (layer-dynamic), plus Full-Cache and a random-eviction control, all with block-granular eviction so FlashAttention is usable. For each bundle: (a) query-aware run — re-score/evict per query, the literature protocol; (b) query-agnostic run — compress once with no query, serve all K. Measure accuracy at K=1 (sanity: must match published numbers within ~2 pts, else our reimplementation is wrong and we stop), then at K∈{4,8,16,32} report tax(K) = acc_queryaware(K) − acc_queryagnostic(K). Hypothesis is falsified if tax < 5% at 12% budget for K=8. (2) RANKING REVERSAL VIA AMORTIZED COST. Plot the Pareto frontier of accuracy vs peak KV memory, and separately accuracy vs GPU-memory-seconds per answered query, at K∈{1,8,32}. Report whether method orderings change between the single-request frontier and the amortized frontier (Kendall tau). (3) PREDICTIVE DIAGNOSTIC: CROSS-QUERY OVERLAP. For every bundle, with zero generation, run the K queries through the compressor's scorer and compute mean pairwise Jaccard overlap of retained KV positions, plus overlap vs a query-agnostic prior. Report Spearman correlation between overlap and tax over all (method, bundle) pairs, and the per-layer overlap profile (predicting that overlap falls in deeper layers, consistent with PyramidKV's own pyramidal observation — this is the paper's own 'not new' observation turned into a reusability diagnostic). If correlation > 0.6, practitioners get a cheap pre-check. (4) SIMPLE QUERY-AGNOSTIC INTERVENTION. One baseline: score KV entries by ||v|| (value activation norm, the signal reviewers flagged as ignored), keep block-aligned top-B per layer with a layer budget profile taken from a *dev-only* grid search (one small dev split, never the test bundles), plus the K=1 sanity and a random-budget ablation. Test whether it shrinks tax(K) at matched budget and whether it beats query-agnostic PyramidKV/DynamicKV/LAVa, i.e. whether the tax is a protocol artifact or a genuine limitation of attention-score scoring. Optional ablation: hybrid core-cache + per-query recomputation of top-r evicted blocks, to see how much of the tax is cheaply recoverable (r/K sensitivity). (5) FLASHTATTENTION / SYSTEMS CHECK. Verify all compressors run in a paged block-sparse kernel path; report TTFT and resident KV bytes, so the reviewer-flagged incompatibility concern is measured rather than argued. Metrics: EM/F1 and substring-match accuracy per task family; tax(K); normalized accuracy retention; mean pairwise Jaccard overlap; Spearman/Kendall correlations; peak KV bytes; TTFT; amortized accuracy per GPU-memory-second; all with 3 seeds where generation is stochastic and bootstrap CIs over bundles.
draft.limitations: (i) Reimplementation risk: reproducing PyramidKV/DynamicKV/LAVa numbers within 2 pts is required, and a failed K=1 sanity check is itself informative but may consume time; plan for ~2 of 8 GPU-days on calibration. (ii) Query diversity is the crux; if our K queries are near-duplicates the tax vanishes trivially and the hypothesis is unfalsified rather than supported — we therefore pre-register a diversity criterion (answer spans in disjoint document regions) and report the overlap distribution so the reader can judge. (iii) Confound between compression budget and reusability: a method could be weak in both regimes; the relative tax (matched budget, same method) controls for this but not perfectly for ceiling effects near saturated accuracy — we include a low-budget arm (5%) to move off ceiling. (iv) Only two 7–8B models and ≤64k contexts; conclusions about 128k+ or MoE models are extrapolations. (v) The value-norm baseline is intentionally simple; if it wins, the 'contribution' is partly a well-known signal revived in a new protocol, so we frame it as protocol diagnosis, not a SOTA method claim. (vi) The overlap diagnostic is method-dependent and may be uninformative for quantization-based compressors (PolarQuant, MiniKV) where 'positions retained' is not the right abstraction; we scope the diagnostic to eviction/selection methods and say so. (vii) Amortized-cost analysis depends on assumed K and batching; we report curves rather than a single K. (viii) No proprietary weights or future papers are used, so nothing here relies on answer keys.

draft.analysis.aggregation: Average decoding replicates within each prompt first, then compute prompt-level paired differences. Model and task summaries are means of prompt-level differences; never treat decoding replicates as independent. Report exploratory multi-document QA separately.

draft.analysis.exclusion_rules[1]: Exclude a run cell from contrast if tensor-level total KV bytes differ from B beyond the pre-registered accounting tolerance, tokenized context length or dtype differs, the full-cache reference is missing, or label or reference leakage into prompts is detected; report every exclusion.
